title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
text:
For three years I ran a deliberate, badly-controlled optimization experiment on myself: stopped stimulants, added supplements, rebuilt my gym routine, worked on sleep and wore a Whoop continuously throughout to measure whether any of it worked.
This is the analysis of that record: 1007 consecutive days (Aug 2023 – Aug 2026), treated as a measurement problem rather than a health story.
The short answer to “which of my optimisations worked”: the largest effect in three years of data was a variable I had never modelled, and the most interesting intermediate result turned out to be an artifact of a hardware upgrade.

Built a reproducible pipeline from a raw multi-file export to a one-row-per-day analysis table (one row that contains daily metrics values), and found two silent bugs that had been corrupting every result
Identified the largest single driver of my sleep duration, and it was a variable the device records automatically and never asks about
Reverse-engineered the rolling-baseline behaviour of the vendor’s recovery score, produced a fitted model that predicted a three-year trend from daily variation
Developed an empirical-null placebo calibration for detecting structural breaks in autocorrelated self-tracked series
Full estimation stack: Newey–West (HAC) standard errors, month fixed effects, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR

The most useful output is the negative one. A result that survives every within-sample diagnostic can still be an artifact of the instrument, and this project is a worked example of catching that.

title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
text:
The Data
The raw export is four files at different grains:



File
Rows
Grain




physiological_cycles.csv
1,009
one physiological cycle


sleeps.csv
1,110
one sleep, naps separated


workouts.csv
1,038

journal_entries.csv
12,206

These merge into 1,007 daily rows covering 94% of the calendar days in the span. Outcomes are HRV, resting heart rate, recovery score, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and the full sleep-stage breakdown.

title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
section: Data Preparation, and Two Bugs That Mattered
text:
Data Preparation, and Two Bugs That Mattered
This section is most of the actual work, and it is where the project nearly died without anyone noticing.

A “day” does not start at midnight
A physiological cycle begins at sleep onset, not at 00:00. I verified this directly against the export: Cycle start time equals Sleep onset exactly on every row that has both. A cycle runs from falling asleep to falling asleep again, and its recovery score describes the day you wake into.
That has a consequence most people will hit and not see:

I am a late sleeper: 827 of 1,009 cycles begin between midnight and 5am, where cycle-start date and the day described are the same
But 171 cycles begin between 21:00 and 23:59, and every one collides on the calendar with the cycle that legitimately owns that date
My first pipeline keyed on cycle-start date and called drop_duplicates(keep="first")

That silently deleted 115 cycles, 113 of them early-bedtime nights, and they were not a random 11%:




kept
silently dropped




mean recovery
58.9
66.3


mean sleep
386 min
454 min



It was discarding my best-rested, longest-sleep nights, in a way correlated with the exposures I was studying. The fix: join on the cycle-start timestamp, which is cycle identity rather than a date and matches exactly across all four files, then label each row by the calendar date of wake onset. Two collisions instead of 115. 113 days recovered.
No error was raised at any point. It is one line doing exactly what it was told.


Missing journal answers are two different things
Journal questions were rolled out in batches, so a question has no rows at all before its launch date. Separately, the prompt goes unanswered on ~22% of cycles.
Neither is filled with False. A day before a question existed is not a verified “no”, and neither is a skipped prompt. Both stay NaN so every model’s dropna() removes them. An earlier version filled them with False instead, which turns a comparison of eras into what looks like a comparison of behaviours.

title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
text:
Statistical Approach
Three problems are structural in this kind of data. Each has one fix.

Autocorrelation. Today’s HRV is highly predictable from yesterday’s, so ordinary regression thinks it has ~900 independent facts when it has far fewer, and returns error bars that are too narrow. → Newey–West (HAC) standard errors, one-week lag window. Point estimates unchanged; uncertainty made honest.
Slow confounding. Behaviour is not randomly assigned across a life: habits, training and stress move in multi-month blocks, so any pooled contrast is partly “2025 vs 2026”. → Month fixed effects, which force every comparison to happen within a calendar month and absorb anything moving slower than that. Months containing only exposed or only unexposed days are dropped, since they carry no within-month contrast.
Multiple comparisons. The project runs well over a hundred tests, which buys about five free discoveries at p < 0.05. → Benjamini–Hochberg FDR, reported as q within each family.

Every model is fit twice, naive and within-month, and both are reported. The gap between them is itself a result: it measures how much of an apparent effect was era.
Deliberately not used: no PCA, no mixed models, no machine learning. Every question here is “does this exposure shift this one outcome,” with one subject and n in the hundreds. OLS with the right standard errors and the right fixed effects answers that exactly; anything heavier would add opacity without adding identification.

title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
text:
What the Models Showed

Sleep timing dominates everything else
The variable I had never modelled turned out to be the largest one available.

Compensation: for each hour later I fall asleep, I wake only 0.40 hours later (95% CI 0.24–0.56). I recover 40% of a late night and lose the rest
Net cost: roughly 24 minutes of sleep per hour of delay (95% CI −28.8 to −18.5, n = 974)
Relative scale: bedtime alone explains 15.1% of the variance in sleep duration; month fixed effects season, fitness, life phase, hardware explain 4.9%
Dose-response: monotone across six bedtime bins spanning 136 minutes end to end
Composition: light sleep absorbs 63% of the loss, REM 25%, slow-wave only 11%




Sleep duration by bedtime bin against a 01:00–02:00 reference, and the stage decomposition of the loss. Within-month, adjusted for training load, Newey–West standard errors, 95% CIs.


That last point is a validity check rather than a finding, and it is the one I like most. Deep sleep being defended while light sleep is cut is the textbook homeostatic hierarchy under sleep restriction: reproduced here by a wrist device inferring stages from photoplethysmography and an accelerometer. It does not make the staging accurate in absolute terms. It does say the errors are not large enough to wash out real structure.
Two nulls worth reporting: rolling 7-day variability in sleep onset adds nothing once the level is known (p = 0.39 / 0.79 / 0.93 for duration, recovery, HRV). And there is no rebound: a short night is not repaid the next night (p = 0.32).


Illness is detectable early and still useless as an alarm
Converting each biomarker to a personal rolling 30-day z-score, with the window shifted so today is never inside its own baseline, and counting only the first day of each episode (28 onsets from 108 flagged days):

HRV sits at z = −0.63 three days before onset against +0.04 on control days, q = 0.005
A composite index over the pre-onset window gives Cohen’s d = 0.37, p = 0.004

The signal is real. The product is not: a threshold catching 57% of illnesses costs about 76 false alarms a year, one every five days. Tighten it to one false alarm a month and you catch one illness in seven.
A statistically significant biomarker and a usable clinical alert are completely different bars. That gap is why a company can publish a true early-detection result and still not ship the feature.

title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
text:
The Result That Didn’t Survive
The headline finding of an earlier version of this project was that the vendor’s recovery score, computed against a rolling personal baseline, has a negative long-run sensitivity to HRV: responding to sustained change backwards. A fitted transfer function located a 30-day baseline window and predicted the observed multi-year drift quantitatively (+2.3 pts/yr predicted, +1.68 observed).
It does not survive a device-generation split.



Fit
n
Long-run sensitivity (pts/ms)
95% CI




Pooled
967
−0.281
−0.426 to −0.136


Older hardware
704
−0.273
−0.523 to −0.022


Newer hardware
256
+0.686
+0.269 to +1.104

298
+0.048
−0.547 to +0.643



The sign flips, and the newer-hardware interval excludes both zero and the pooled estimate. The descriptive paradox behind it was never significant either (between-quarter r = −0.29, p = 0.34, 13 quarters); at monthly resolution the correlation is positive inside both eras and null when pooled.
The mechanism is a single offset: the newer device reads mean HRV 69.0 ms against 91.4, while giving a higher mean recovery score.



Left: monthly means, coloured by device generation. The positive within-era relationship (+0.43 and +0.68) vanishes when the two are pooled. Right: the fitted long-run sensitivity by era, 95% CIs, Newey–West. The sign flips across the hardware change, and the cleanest single year is a null.


Two offset clouds, one regression line, and a slope that describes neither of them.

The method that catches it
The transferable piece is the calibration, not the failure.

Take the discontinuity estimator and run it at 400 randomly chosen cut-dates across the record
That gives the distribution of jumps this specific autocorrelated series produces where nothing happened
Score the real date against it

On resting heart rate at the device swap, a naive t-test gives p < 0.0001; the empirical null says a jump that big appears in 18% of random splits. Three orders of magnitude of overconfidence, all from autocorrelation. On HRV at the same date, the observed step is smaller than random splits produce 66% of the time: nothing at all.
A method that ranks a real artifact far from a non-artifact, rather than confirming everything, is the useful kind.
Supporting this: across a documented sequence of personal changes preceding the hardware swap, my resting heart rate is flat (53.3 → 52.4 → 54.2 → 54.6 bpm, no step significant) and then jumps +4.7 bpm at the device change alone.



Four consecutive periods, each differing from the last by one documented change, all on the same hardware, then a device replacement. The two headline metrics fail in opposite directions, which is the worst possible arrangement: a naive before-and-after averages a real physiological signal with a pure instrument artifact.


Months of deliberate change, no movement; one afternoon with a different strap, four and a half beats.

title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
text:
Limitations
Stated plainly, because they are the reason this is a portfolio project and not a paper.

n = 1. Nothing here generalises to people. It generalises, at most, to method.
Sleep duration is partly an accounting identity with bedtime and wake time. The empirical content is the 40% compensation coefficient, not the 24 minutes, which partly follows from it.
The device timestamps sleep onset, not lights-out. A night spent awake in bed is indistinguishable from a night that simply started late, and this dataset can never separate them. An earlier version of this analysis claimed a falsification test had ruled that out; the test was inverted, since high sleep pressure predicts exactly the consolidation pattern I had treated as evidence against it.
Everything is observational. Bedtime is chosen, not assigned. The next step is a pre-registered, block-randomised, placebo-blinded crossover on a single lever, the only design here that could settle a cause.
Effect sizes are not stable across device generations, which is the whole point of the section above.

title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
text:
What It Actually Concluded
Ranked by effect size, across three years of things I deliberately changed and one thing I never thought to measure:







Lever
Effect on nightly sleep




Bedtime, 25th → 75th percentile
−57 min


Moving apartment
+47 min


Screens in bed
−25.7 min


Melatonin
confounded by indication: I take it on nights I expect to sleep badly


Morning light, meditation
no comparison group; compliance too high to estimate anything



This is n = 1 and it does not generalise. It is not health advice and I would be annoyed at anyone reading it as such. What it supports is a claim about method: that a single subject with enough observations and careful enough estimation can identify which of their own levers matter. It is not a claim about people.
But it is my n of 1, and for a decision about my own life that is often the more relevant number. The ordering above says I had my priorities backwards: I spent three years adding and removing things, measuring carefully, while the largest available lever sat underneath all of it, unmeasured.
My sister is a psychiatrist and has been giving me this advice for free for years: first things first. Before you add stuff, take stuff away, or buy supplements, work on your sleep. It took a thousand nights of data, one false positive, and a lot of Newey–West standard errors to reproduce what she said over dinner.

title: Three Years of My Own Wearable Data
section: Where I’d like to take this next
text:
Where I’d like to take this next

Log lights-out time. One button press a night, and it resolves the largest open limitation.
Run the randomised crossover. Pre-registered, ~102 nights per arm from this dataset’s own residual variance, roughly seven months.
Treat the current hardware era as day zero of a clean series: one instrument, no structural break, still growing.

If you work on digital biomarkers, wearable signal validity, or n-of-1 methodology, or you build these devices and want an outside read on how the longitudinal record behaves, my contact details are at the bottom of this page.
Raw data stays on my machine. Numbers reported here are summaries, not rows.

title: Early Detection of COVID-19 Using Wearable Device Data
text:
In this project, I explored whether physiological data from consumer wearable devices such as heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, activity, etc… can be used to predict COVID-19 infection before symptom onset.

Implemented a sliding-window algorithm on publicly available wearable datasets

Achieved early detection performance of around 80% up to ~5 days before symptom onset (proof-of-concept level)
Built an end-to-end pipeline from data ingestion to anomaly detection

Turned the work into an award-winning startup concept, winning the Big Idea Challenge at the University of North Dakota and reaching the finals of the Middleton School of Entrepreneurship business plan competition

title: Early Detection of COVID-19 Using Wearable Device Data
text:
Problem Background
During the COVID-19 pandemic, most screening relied on:

Spot checks (temperature, pulse oximetry)
Lab tests (PCR, antigen)
Self-reported symptoms

These are often:

Late (after symptoms appear)

Infrequent (once a day, or only when people feel sick)

Sometimes inconvenient or expensive

At the same time, many people already wear devices that continuously capture signals closely tied to early illness:

Resting heart rate (RHR)
Heart rate variability (HRV)
Sleep disruption
Activity patterns

Previous studies have shown that changes in these metrics can precede SARS-CoV-2 symptom onset by several days. My goal was to turn these ideas into a concrete, reproducible modeling pipeline, and then explore what a real product around this might look like.

title: Early Detection of COVID-19 Using Wearable Device Data
text:
Technical Approach

Data & Signals
I worked with publicly available wearable datasets where:

Participants wore smartwatches or similar devices for multiple months

The data included RHR, HRV, steps, and sleep metrics
COVID-19 infection dates and symptom onset days were known or approximated

This allowed me to:

Align time series around infection (“day 0” = symptom onset / diagnosis)
Study patterns in the days leading up to infection
Prototype detection algorithms without needing to run my own large prospective study



Modeling

Preprocesses the time-series data

Normalize signals (e.g., resting heart rate deviations from personal baseline)
Handle missing data and noisy segments

Slices the data into overlapping windows

Windows of fixed length (e.g., several days)
Slide forward one day at a time
Each window is labeled relative to infection status (pre-infection, infection, or healthy period)

Extracts features per window

Baseline-adjusted RHR
Short-term and long-term HRV statistics
Sleep duration and interruptions
Activity changes (e.g., steps)

Detects anomalies

Compares each window to that person’s usual patterns
Flags periods where signals deviate significantly
Aggregates anomalies to mark potential “early warning” zones

Evaluates performance

Measures how often warning periods overlap with the days leading up to infection
Reports sensitivity/recall for detecting infection in advance
Compares performance across different feature sets (RHR only vs. multi-signal)


The modeling approach is directly inspired by prior work (e.g., RHR-Diff and HROS-AD style methods) but focuses on multi-signal integration and sliding-window framing as a clean way to think about early detection.

title: Early Detection of COVID-19 Using Wearable Device Data
section: Developing the Venture Around the Technology
text:
Developing the Venture Around the Technology
Although this started as a research exercise, it quickly grew into a startup-oriented concept.

Big Idea Challenge – 1st Prize
I used this project to participate in the Big Idea Challenge at the University of North Dakota and won first place.
In that context, I:

Defined the product as a digital health platform that:

Integrates with existing wearables
Computes early-risk scores for COVID-like infections
Provides dashboards for users and potentially clinicians

Highlighted key differentiators:

Focus on pre-symptomatic detection, not just monitoring
Ability to integrate new signals (temperature, SpO₂) as devices evolve
Potential extension beyond COVID-19 to broader infectious diseases

Presented:

A business model (subscription / B2B2C SaaS)
A rough product roadmap (from proof-of-concept to validated medical device)
Early thoughts about regulatory and clinical validation


Some of the slides I used in that pitch included:

An “80% prediction 5 days early” result summary

A market overview of the wearable and remote patient monitoring space

A competition and unique value proposition (UVP) slide showing how this sits next to Apple, Google, and other digital health companies

A roadmap slide outlining steps toward integrating with third-party devices, developing dedicated hardware, and pursuing FDA clearance



Middleton School of Entrepreneurship – Finalist
Later, I expanded the idea into a 30-page business plan and became a finalist in the UND Middleton School of Entrepreneurship Business Plan Competition.
In that process, I:

Conducted market analysis (TAM/SAM/SOM, key players, trends in remote patient monitoring and digital biomarkers)
Defined a go-to-market strategy (clinical partners, pilot projects, early adopters)
Built financial projections
Outlined a regulatory and validation path:

Clinical trials
Partnerships with hospitals / clinics
Steps toward FDA clearance and broader deployment


I am not publishing the business plan text here, but it is available upon request in the right context (e.g., for serious collaboration or review).
UND Biomedical Research Conference Poster (2021)

title: Brain-Controlled Robot for Assisting Basic Upper Limb Tasks
text:
This was my first real introduction to BCI and EEG work.
The idea was simple: can we use a hobby-grade portable EEG sensor to control a robotic arm?
I wanted to explore whether basic EEG signals can trigger simple robotic actions using thought-linked gestures. It was an early experiment, but it showed that even low-cost EEG hardware can drive meaningful control of assistive devices.

Overview

Conference Demo: IEEE Body Sensor Networks (BSN) 2023

Collaborators: Dr. Mohammad Arif Ul Alam (UMass Lowell), Dr. João Luís G. Rosa (University of São Paulo)

Hardware: Muse 2 EEG headband, Raspberry Pi-based robotic arm

Objective: Upper-limb motion control via low-cost, portable EEG interface




System Design
The system converts raw EEG signals (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, theta) into control commands using a threshold-based event detector.
A Raspberry Pi processes classified EEG inputs and drives the robotic arm’s motors through serial communication.








What I Learned & Why It Was Hard
Training a model to “detect thoughts” with a hobby EEG device is extremely difficult.
Because the Muse 2 only has four electrodes, all placed on the frontal lobe, the signals mainly reflect:

Focus

Attention

Facial muscle movement

But intentional movement comes from the motor cortex, which is located at the top of the head…
far away from where the Muse collects data. This meant true “thought-based motion classification” wasn’t realistic with this device, and the model I made was really just overfitting to my brain patterns, as well as the limited scope of classifying only two distinct motions. On the other hand, blinking and jaw clench events were very easy to implement.


















Impact & Future Work
Now that I better understand the relationship between brain regions and movement intention, the next step is clear:

Move from 4 frontal electrodes → to multi-channel EEG covering the motor cortex

Try a portable headset like the Emotiv Epoc X, which actually places electrodes over the movement areas

Re-run the study with better spatial coverage

Eventually test it in rehabilitation or assistive-tech contexts

In the end, I did discover a really interesting use-case for the Muse. Because the frontal lobe signals are more about focus, it’s actually much better suited for studying attention and mental engagement. Doing deep work or the idea of being in a flow state, or what athletes call “in the zone.” I even ran a small focus study around this concept, which you can check out here.



Resources

Code Repository: GitHub – NazimBL/EEG-Controlled-Robot

Publication: ResearchGate Article




Demo Video – EEG-Controlled Robotic Arm (BSN 2023)

title: My AI Setup: A Second Brain That Reads Like a Repo
text:
The TLDR:
What?: I put together a script that scans a year of scattered notes, research, and projects, tags them, links them, and compiles the result into a wiki any LLM can read.
So what? If you’ve had an AI assistant or chatbot, sometimes you notice it loses the thread of a long conversation, focuses on the wrong things, or forgets everything the second a new session starts. It’s not only long chats — point Claude Code, Codex, or any coding assistant at a real project and you hit the same wall from the other side: you’re either uploading way more files than the question needs, or hunting through folders trying to guess which one gives enough “context.”
Now what?: Every model I open now gets the same context without me re-explaining myself, none of that memory depends on one company or model, and nothing about my research or my ideas has to leave my machine to get useful answers.

title: My AI Setup: A Second Brain That Reads Like a Repo
text:
The problem
You’ve felt this even if you’ve never called it “context engineering.” A long chat with ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Claude, or Gemini starts overfitting to some random fragment from five messages ago. When you haven’t set it up to remember anything, it goes the other way: full amnesia every session, re-explain yourself from zero.
Neither is a model-capability problem. It’s just that nothing survives the scroll. The thing that mattered in message two is diluted by message forty, and the model has no way to tell load-bearing context from noise.

title: My AI Setup: A Second Brain That Reads Like a Repo
text:
Enter: the Compiler
I got the main idea from the now well-popular Andrej Karpathy LLM wiki repo. The main takeaway from the approach described in his gist was that the correct way to use an LLM over your own knowledge isn’t Q&A, it’s compilation. Raw material (files, code, notes) stays untouched. The LLM’s job is to read it and maintain a separate, structured layer on top: a wiki that gets rebuilt, not a chat log that gets scrolled past.
Anyone who’s used a coding agent already knows why it works: those tools are noticeably better inside a real repo than in a stray folder of scripts, because a repo carries structure the model can navigate — file layout, imports, a README, commit history. A year of notes is the same raw material, just unstructured. Compiling turns it into something with the shape of a repo: tagged, cross-linked, indexed.

title: My AI Setup: A Second Brain That Reads Like a Repo
text:
How I built mine
Obsidian started as a local, markdown-based note-taking app. It turned into an actual knowledge base once there was enough in it, and from there it was a short step to wiring that knowledge base into an LLM directly.
I connected Obsidian to my home folder (referred to as “Vault”), then split it into three top-level folders: Atlas/ for concepts and general notes, Projects/ for ventures and builds, Research/ for research and PhD-level material.
On top of that sits a compiler I wrote. It scans the whole vault, finds tags and shared attributes, flags notes talking about the same thing from different folders, and writes a report. A root CLAUDE.md reads that report and does the actual tagging and linking pass, then compiles a second layer: the Wiki/ layer — one page per tag, plus concept pages that pull a single subject together across folders instead of leaving it scattered as unrelated notes.

title: My AI Setup: A Second Brain That Reads Like a Repo
text:
CLAUDE.md (or planner.md) as a router
Each project folder also gets its own scoped CLAUDE.md, a local router, separate from the root one. A coding project I’m building doesn’t need the same CLAUDE.md as the wiki compiler, and it definitely doesn’t need the one sitting in my EEG research folder, which is overfitted to EEG-specific knowledge. Each one stays scoped to its own folder instead of leaking into the others. One general CLAUDE.md, a planner.md, and a memory.md aren’t enough on their own — I found that scoping them per-folder is what actually solves the context problem described above.
Adding to this, I’ve also got a small set of specialist agents sitting on top of the same vault (researcher, software engineer, task manager). I use them two ways: called by name directly in Claude Code, or run through a script that translates the agent files so they work with other models too.

title: My AI Setup: A Second Brain That Reads Like a Repo
section: Extra payoffs that matter as much as the wiki itself
text:
Extra payoffs that matter as much as the wiki itself
It’s model-agnostic. In my opinion (which could be just paranoia), current pricing for what tools like Claude Code and Codex can do is mostly labs racing each other for market share. I’m not convinced those prices and that accessibility will hold. Everything here is plain markdown, nothing locked into one vendor’s format. My daily driver is a base Claude subscription; when I run out of credits, Gemini CLI and a couple of local models pick up the slack. Point the whole setup at a different provider and nothing about the vault needs to be rebuilt.
It’s actually private. Nothing here depends on uploading research notes or half-formed ideas to a chatbot to get an answer. The vault lives in a private repo, and the compiler runs locally against files on my own machine.

title: My AI Setup: A Second Brain That Reads Like a Repo
text:
The second brain
I’ve spent a lot of time trying to figure out the best AI tools and combinations to actually use day to day. This is the one that stuck: markdown notes, a compiler, and a wiki layer sitting on top of both. One place, one source of truth, a lot less friction picking which tool or model to use, and a lot less re-explaining myself to whatever model I happen to have open.
The app I take notes in is now also my knowledge base and the repo I actually work from. I still run WSL with VS Code open next to Obsidian, but almost everything I do, day to day, happens in a terminal now.
Which brings me to the Obsidian Graph view itself. I didn’t build it — it’s just what shows up once enough notes are actually linked. It’s probably the main reason this whole second-brain trend got so popular in the first place: it looks cool. Can’t lie, I was glazing the first time I saw one. Turns out it’s not just eye candy, though — a model reasoning over an explicit graph knowledge base has less room to invent a connection that isn’t actually there (GraphRAG, if you’re curious, or iykyk).

title: My thoughts on AI and Agent Coding tools
text:
I was glad when a friend sent me this post by Andrej Karpathy,
which basically says programming is being refactored so fast by agents and new workflows that even top engineers feel behind, and not learning to use these “alien” tools effectively now feels like a skill issue.
I felt a short relief to know that one of the most popular voices in the AI field feels this way. I was kind of overwhelmed by all the different possibilities to improve my coding and research productivity. Before discussing this, I was in the process of resetting my laptop and thought I would update my IDEs and coding environment for the new year. It’s not only hard to keep up with the new tools and products that are coming out, but also how to use them.

title: My thoughts on AI and Agent Coding tools
text:
What My Research Said
I asked a couple of friends in industry around the world (software and AI engineers/developers), and of course did a “deep research” on both ChatGPT 5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro. Both were unanimous on Cursor, with honorable mentions like Windsurf and Zed. This corresponds to the response of my smart friends (shout out to Dr. Nezih and Patrick, first is a PhD, second is a machine learning engineer). Someone should ask Claude and see what Claude Code thinks about all this.
The TLDR:
Cursor is the superior IDE choice, plus some extensions I never heard of (Ruff, Marimo).
for Local inference (privacy) : ollama running deepseek-coder-v2 connected back to Cursor

Stronger “agent-centric” UX
Great for multi-file refactors and feature work in research codebases
Free tier exists but is limited; heavy agent use typically pushes you to pay subscription

Note: I got these results by giving details about the workflows I develop and my research, so expect to get different responses with different prompting details.
I believe it will still be hard to define “the best tools” given the difficulties mentioned in the post above and the intensity of AI agent competition. While I was writing this, I took a break and came across an article about Meta acquiring Magnus, a Chinese startup that has advanced agent intelligence that can independently research, plan, and execute multiple tasks.
With all this being said, programming and coding, in my opinion, can be as subjective as driving a car. Here’s how I see it: agents in coding are like AI-assisted driving, Vibe coding on the other hand is like automatic gear cars. It’s still necessary to be able to have control and take control of the wheels, while some enjoy the old-fashioned manual gear.
This analogy doesn’t hold in terms of productivity though. I’m 100% convinced that agent/AI-helped coding can and will make us exponentially better, faster, and more productive. It’s a matter of how much and how as well as picking the right tools that fit you, and not being left behind.

The verification flow with video recording, it just opens a browser and tests the code live. The Antigravity browser control extension’s auto-debugging is insane and pretty unique in my experience. title: About
text:
Welcome to my website! I’m an engineer-scientist working on translational biomedical AI. See my CV for details.

Short Bio
Fluent in both human and programming languages, Nazim holds a B.S. in Electrical and Electronics Engineering and an M.Eng. in Computer Engineering from the University of Boumerdès Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineering. He worked as an Embedded Software Engineer and later co-founded Deadline Technologies and Deadline Store, gaining hands-on experience in prototyping and product development. After completing a year of biomedical engineering and research studies at the University of North Dakota, he joined the University of Massachusetts Lowell, where he earned an M.S. and Ph.D in Computer Science. His research sits at the intersection of embedded systems, AI, and human biology. He is currently a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research (CVVR) at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), a Harvard Medical School teaching hospital in Boston, where he builds GPU-accelerated multi-omics pipelines and AI models that connect molecular data to disease mechanisms.


Brief Summary on My Research
My research focuses on understanding biomedical phenomena and identifying key biomarkers that distinguish physiological states, behaviors, or disease conditions. I apply artificial intelligence (coupled with this understandings not as a black box) to uncover meaningful patterns in complex health data. My work spans the full pipeline: from designing and prototyping sensor-integrated wearable devices for biomarker acquisition, to data analysis, modeling, and real-time AI deployment.
I have expertise in electronics design, embedded systems, data science, machine learning, and generative AI (diffusion models). I develop computational and edge-AI solutions for health monitoring and diagnosis. You can see more about my research on my Research Page.


Entrepreneurship & Innovation
I’ve participated in several entrepreneurial and product-driven engineering efforts. In 2019 I co-founded Deadline Technologies, where I produced development boards for academic and industrial use. This experience involved full product lifecycle: PCB design, firmware, marketing, and direct sales. I also co-founded Deadline Store, an electronics retail and community initiative that helped make maker tools and components more accessible to students and builders in Algeria.


Quantitative Trading & Market Analysis
When I need a break from research, I analyze financial markets: price action, time-series modeling, and how expectations about future moves get priced into options (IV). I built an automated TradingView generator that visualizes expected moves from option chain data. It’s a hobby, but it runs on the same loop as my research: identifying patterns, testing hypotheses, building models, and evaluating them over time.
Outside research, I enjoy going to the gym, watching sports, traveling, writing, and I like to think I’m pretty good at soccer and pool.
If you made this far, thank you ! your attention is much appreciated in an age full of noise.
Nazim.

title: Scholar Agent Room: multi-agent room for scientific brainstorming
text: This post is the first in a series on “Agentic AI Programming” where I’ll experiment with different tools, agents, and ADKs (Agent Development Kits) I’ve tried. I will be sharing my experience compared to how the tools are advertized.

title: Scholar Agent Room: multi-agent room for scientific brainstorming
text:
The New Era of Creation
I always thought coding was like having a super power. But this brings content and software creation to the next level (no wonder why the stock market is freaking out). I can’t remember the last time I was this excited about creating and developing solutions.
At the same time, I feel a little bit frustrated that I don’t have enough time to test, and evaluate every idea I have. I’m in the last semester of my PhD, facing tons of obligations. The frustration persists because I see so many people doing cool things despite their obligations, so I can’t find excuses. I just don’t want to be left behind. (Note: some of the things I wrote in my previous post are already kind of deprecated! That’s how fast things move.)

title: Scholar Agent Room: multi-agent room for scientific brainstorming
text:
Enter: Scholar Agent Room
Since I was working on some grant writing, I decided to take the opportunity to investigate a specific aspect of Agentic AI: Multi-Agent Conversational Systems. I read good things about AutoGen in the scope of conversational chat rooms, so that’s what I decided to go with for this project.
The result is the ScholarAgentRoom — an expert multi-agent room designed specifically for scientific brainstorming.



Scholar Agent Room Interface



What it does
The goal was to build a system that could act as a rigorous scientific panel. I set up four specialized agents, each with focused system prompts to simulate a real academic review board:

BioExpert: Focuses on mechanistic plausibility and experimental feasibility.
AIExpert: Handles data requirements, modeling strategies, and evaluation metrics.
Reviewer: Adopts an “NIH-style” rigor to provide critical feedback and identify weaknesses.
GrantsWriter: Ensures clarity, significance, and proper innovation framing.



Modes of Operation
I wanted flexibility, so I implemented two modes:

Freestyle: A more relaxed, open-ended discussion where agents freely exchange ideas.
Evidence Mode: This is where it gets interesting. Agents are forced to structure their critiques using a strict framework: Claim – Evidence – Risk – Improvement – Confidence. This prevents hallucination and vague feedback.



Privacy and Architecture
One critical aspect of this project was privacy. We do not want our research ideas flying off to a public API log somewhere.
I set up the infrastructure to run on a remote GPU cluster, accessed securely via an SSH tunnel. The local UI connects through this tunnel to the backend on the cluster, which then talks to a local LLM server. This ensures that while I use a nice web interface locally, the heavy lifting happens on the cluster, and everything stays private and encrypted.

title: Scholar Agent Room: multi-agent room for scientific brainstorming
text:
Future Work
Like everything in this space, this project could have so many iterations and directions. The repository itself lists plenty of future enhancements, from “Agent Memory” to “Team Variants” like swarm behaviors.
I’m really looking forward to seeing what my fellow collaborators and professors think about it. It’s an experimental tool, but it feels like a glimpse into how we’ll all be doing research fundamentally different in the very soon.
Check out the code and the full breakdown on the repo:
github.com/NazimBL/ScholarAgentRoom

title: I Optimised Everything for Three Years. But all I had to fix was Bedtime.
text:
I view the human body as the most complex engineered system we know, and for three years I treated my own like one. I wore a Whoop every night from August 2023 to August 2026 and ran an ongoing, badly-controlled experiment on myself.
I stopped stimulants. I added supplements and melatonin, the usual list. I rebuilt my gym routine more than once. I worked on sleep hygiene: no screens in bed, ear plugs, morning light, meditation. Every one of those the Whoop app asks you about each morning, and I answered honestly for a thousand mornings.
Then I exported the whole record : 1009 cycles (whoop daily records), 1110 sleeps, 1038 workouts, 12,206 journal answers and asked the obvious question. Which of these actually did anything?
The answer took a detour through a result that turned out to be an illusion, and then landed somewhere I was not expecting and had never measured.

title: I Optimised Everything for Three Years. But all I had to fix was Bedtime.
text:
The detour
The first thing I noticed was not about my habits at all.
Over three years my HRV (Heart rate variability) fell by 8.3 ms (milliseconds) per year, from 97 ms to 65 ms by quarter. A third of it, gone. My recovery score (The Whoop metric that measures “freshness/readiness”) over the same period went up by 1.7 points a year.
That is not a rounding error. HRV is the biggest single input to that score. One number said I had lost a third of my stress-regulation capacity (lower HRV); the other said I was very slightly better than before (higher recovery).
Then the comparison that made me sit up. Within a quarter, HRV and recovery correlate at r = +0.80: day to day, the score tracks HRV almost perfectly. Between quarters, r = −0.29. Over long spans the relationship doesn’t just weaken. It inverts.
I had a mechanism ready. The score is computed against a rolling personal baseline, so it answers “how are you today versus your recent self,” and it re-baselines continuously. As your recent self gets worse, the score quietly redefines what a 60 means.
So I fitted it, recovery as a function of today’s HRV and resting heart rate plus a trailing baseline of each, sweeping the baseline window. The fit peaked sharply at 30 days. Read the two HRV terms together and you get a long-run sensitivity of −0.28 points per millisecond. Negative. Not weak, not noisy: backwards.
Then the check that convinced me. If that model is right, at my measured HRV slope the score should drift up by +2.3 points a year. It actually drifted up by +1.68. A model fitted to daily wobble had predicted a three-year trend it was never shown.
Every diagnostic passed. I thought I had something.

title: I Optimised Everything for Three Years. But all I had to fix was Bedtime.
text:
What killed it
I took a step back and tried to figure out other co-founders or variables, environmental changes I should have considered in the analysis and found the problem: I’d forgotten I switched devices partway through the study, and my model was quietly averaging together three years of data from two different wearables.
My Whoop 4 was swapped for a Whoop 5 about two-thirds of the way through. Split by device instead of pooled together, here’s what the same model shows.



Fit
n
Long-run sensitivity




Pooled all together
967
−0.281


Older device only
704
−0.273


Newer device only
256
+0.686


2024 alone (one device, quiet year)
298
+0.048



The sign flips. And the newer-device interval excludes zero and excludes −0.28, in the opposite direction. The between-quarter r = −0.29 that started the whole thing was never even significant: p = 0.34 on thirteen quarterly means. At monthly resolution, the correlation is positive inside both eras (+0.43 and +0.68) and vanishes when pooled.
Here is the whole mechanism, in two lines:

Older device: mean HRV 91.4 ms, mean recovery 59.0 Newer device: mean HRV 69.0 ms, mean recovery 62.4

The new one reads lower HRV and gives a higher score. Two clouds of points, one shifted down and to the right of the other. Draw a single line through both and the relationship inside each of them disappears.



Each point is one calendar month. Inside each device era the recovery score tracks HRV positively. Pooled across the two, it flattens to nothing, and the transfer function fitted on the pooled record reports a sensitivity with the opposite sign from what the newer device actually shows.


The inversion exists in neither device. It exists only in the union.
The lesson is narrow and usable: before you interpret any long trend in self-tracked data, list every date the instrument could have changed, and refit inside each segment. Hardware swaps, firmware updates, a new sleep-staging model. If a result only exists in the pooled fit, it is a property of the pooling, not of you.

title: I Optimised Everything for Three Years. But all I had to fix was Bedtime.
section: The thing that was actually there
text:
The thing that was actually there
So: back to the original question. Of everything I had deliberately changed over three years, what moved?
Honestly, not much. Screens in bed cost me about 26 minutes of sleep, real, and the largest of the lot. Melatonin looked like it was hurting until I realised I take it on nights I already expect to sleep badly, which reverses the arrow before any model sees the data. Morning light and meditation: nothing I can detect, because I did them nearly every day and left myself no comparison group.
The largest effect in three years of data was in a column I had never opened.
Not one of my models contained the thing the device recorded automatically every single night, on all 974 of them, without ever asking me: what time I actually fell asleep.
When I go to bed an hour later, I wake up only 24 minutes later. I recover 40% of a late night and lose the rest. My wake time isn’t pinned by an alarm, it floats with a standard deviation of 1.8 hours.
That works out to roughly 24 minutes of sleep lost per hour of delay.



Left: sleep duration by bedtime bin, against a 01:00–02:00 reference. Monotone across six bins spanning 136 minutes. Right: where the lost sleep comes from. Deep sleep is defended and light sleep is cut, which is the textbook homeostatic ordering, reproduced here by a wrist sensor.


Bedtime alone explains 15.1% of the variation in my sleep duration. Season, fitness, where I lived, which device I wore, all of it together explains 4.9%.
Three years of optimising, and the biggest lever was the one decision I never wrote down.

title: I Optimised Everything for Three Years. But all I had to fix was Bedtime.
section: The part I couldn’t rule out
text:
The part I couldn’t rule out
The device timestamps sleep onset, not the moment I got into bed. So a night I spent lying awake reading the ceiling looks identical to a night I simply started late. My first draft claimed to have ruled this out: if late nights were insomnia nights, they should carry more wakefulness, and mine carry less.
That argument is backwards, and someone had to show me. The wakefulness the device measures happens after sleep onset. If I’ve been awake for two hours, my sleep pressure is high, so I fall asleep hard and stay asleep. That’s exactly what I saw. The pattern I claimed as proof is the alternative explanation’s own signature.
So some unknown share of my late nights are ordinary bedtimes with bad latency, and this dataset can never separate them. Fixing it needs one variable I don’t have: an actual lights-out time. That’s one button press a night, and I’ve started pressing it.

title: I Optimised Everything for Three Years. But all I had to fix was Bedtime.
text:
What I take from it
This is one person. It is not generalisable, it never was, and I would be annoyed at anyone who read it as health advice.
But it is my n of 1, and for a decision about my own life that is often the more relevant number. What it told me is that I had the order backwards. I spent three years adding things and removing things and measuring the results with a lot of statistical care, and the thing with the biggest effect was sitting underneath all of it, unmeasured, deciding how much of the night I actually got.
My sister is a psychiatrist, and she has been saying a version of this to me for years, for free, without any regressions:

First things first. Before you add stuff, take stuff away, buy supplements: just work on your sleep.

It took me three years, a thousand nights of data, one false positive and a fairly large amount of Newey–West standard errors to arrive at what she said over dinner.
She was right. The full technical write-up (data preparation, the day-boundary bug that silently deleted 11% of my nights, the placebo calibration, and the limitations) is on the project page.
If you read this far, I genuinely appreciate it, thank you, go to bed.

title: MotifXplorer – Genomic Peak Analysis Web Tool
text:
MotifXplorer is now online at this address : motifxplorer.med.und.edu
MotifXplorer is a genomic peak analysis web tool built to help researchers and clinicians analyze transcription factor binding sites (TFBS) from ChIP-seq peak data without having to write code or understand the details of machine learning.
How it works:

Upload your ChIP-seq peak BED file

Let the platform generate negatives, extract sequences, and train an XGBoost model

Get back interpretable results:

Top k-mer–based DNA signatures
Feature importance metrics
Optional motif analysis and decision tree visualization


MotifXplorer was developed in collaboration with Dr. Motoki Takaku’s lab and Mounir Ouadi.

title: MotifXplorer – Genomic Peak Analysis Web Tool
text:
Who is it for?
MotifXplorer is designed for:

Wet-lab biologists and clinicians who work with ChIP-seq peaks and want to explore regulatory patterns

Genomics researchers who don’t have time to build full ML pipelines from scratch

Collaborative teams where some members are non-technical but still need to interpret ML results

The main goal is to lower the barrier to exploring DNA sequence patterns and regulatory elements associated with ChIP-seq peaks.

title: MotifXplorer – Genomic Peak Analysis Web Tool
text:
Demo – Preview of MotifXplorer
Below is a short demo of MotifXplorer running through a typical analysis workflow:
 Your browser does not support the video tag.

title: MotifXplorer – Genomic Peak Analysis Web Tool
text:
Key Capabilities

Genome Selection

Choose from multiple reference genomes:

e.g., hg19, hg38, mm9, and others


The appropriate FASTA is selected behind the scenes so users don’t have to worry about file preparation.



Positive & Negative Examples

Positive set:

Upload a BED file containing your ChIP-seq peaks.

Negative set:

Either upload your own negative BED file, or

Let MotifXplorer automatically generate negatives by sampling genomic regions matched to your positives.


This makes it easy to set up basic supervised classification without manual negative set curation.


XGBoost-Based Analysis
MotifXplorer uses an XGBoost classifier on k-mer–encoded sequences to learn patterns associated with your peaks.
The web tool:

Converts sequences into k-mer features (e.g., k = 4–10)

Trains an XGBoost model

Evaluates performance and exposes:

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score

ROC curve

Feature importances across different metrics




Top Signature DNA Sequences
After training, MotifXplorer extracts and displays:

The top 10 signature DNA sequences (k-mers)

Their importance in classification

How often they contribute to decision splits in the ensemble

This helps highlight candidate regulatory sequence patterns without requiring the user to inspect raw model internals.

title: MotifXplorer – Genomic Peak Analysis Web Tool
text:
Web Workflow
From a user’s perspective, a typical run looks like this:

Select genome

e.g., human (hg19 / hg38) or mouse (mm9).

Upload BED file(s)

Positive ChIP-seq peaks required

Optional negative BED (or let the tool generate it)

Choose k-mer size

Any value in a range like 4–10

Run analysis

XGBoost model trains on-the-fly

Performance metrics and plots are generated

Interpret results

View top k-mers and importance metrics

Optionally run motif analysis

Inspect the decision tree visualization to better understand how the model separates positives vs negatives

title: Immersive VR Rehabilitation for Multiple Sclerosis
text:
The idea is to use immersive virtual reality, bimanual tasks, and haptic/EMG feedback to support rehabilitation for people living with Multiple Sclerosis (MS). The goal is to create a flexible system that can help track progress over time and potentially improve both motor and mental health outcomes.
Because recruiting people with MS and running proper trials is not easy, I haven’t been able to move this project into a full clinical study yet. I’m keeping it here as a detailed case study and an open invitation for collaboration.

title: Immersive VR Rehabilitation for Multiple Sclerosis
section: Enhanced Bimanual Rehabilitation for Multiple Sclerosis using Immersive VR
text:
Enhanced Bimanual Rehabilitation for Multiple Sclerosis using Immersive VR
The concept combines:

A VR headset (immersive environment)

Bimanual tasks (using both hands to perform coordinated actions)

Sensors and haptics, such as EMG and hand-tracking, to collect useful data and provide feedback

The system is built around two VR environments:

Tutorial / assessment environment

Gentle, guided tasks

Focused on learning the interface, assessing reflexes and basic responses

Integrates sensors and haptics for feedback

Realistic scenario (e.g., grocery store simulation)

Everyday bimanual tasks like reaching, grasping, moving items

Designed to be more engaging and closer to daily life

Data from these tasks can be used to monitor changes in performance over time


The idea is to quantify the impact of VR rehab on:

Bimanual function

Activity limitation and participation restriction

Quality of life and possibly MS remission indicators

and compare that to traditional physical therapy approaches.

title: Immersive VR Rehabilitation for Multiple Sclerosis
text:
Research plan (high level)
Even though I haven’t run the full study, I did lay out a research plan that could be picked up by the right team or setting.

Goals

Determine short- and long-term impact of immersive VR rehab on:

Gait and balance

Global motor function

Activity limitation and participation

Cognitive function and mental health


Evaluate whether the VR-based approach offers any added benefit over standard physical therapy

Keep the system low-cost and flexible, so it could be used outside of a single institution



Methodology – concept stage
In a first phase, the plan focuses on:

Bimanual tasks performed in VR, using basic headsets and additional hardware

Collecting diagnostic data such as EMG, hand motion, task completion times, and error patterns

Starting with a proof-of-concept to refine:

Task design

Hardware setup

Data collection pipeline

User comfort and safety


Once the proof-of-concept is stable, the idea is to move toward a pilot study with people living with MS, with proper inclusion criteria, outcome measures, and statistical planning.
Because this involves vulnerable participants and clinical settings, it needs the right environment: IRB support, clinicians, therapists, and access to an MS population. That’s the part I’m currently missing.

title: Immersive VR Rehabilitation for Multiple Sclerosis
text:
What I’ve already done
So far, I’ve:

Written a research proposal and research plan outlining:

Background and literature review on MS and VR rehab

Clear objectives, methodology, and expected outcomes

How to compare VR rehab to traditional therapy


Created and presented a poster at the UND Biomedical Research Conference (2021)

Built a slide deck that walks through:

MS basics (etiology, symptoms, costs, quality of life)

Existing VR rehab work and the current research gap

The system concept and research objectives


These materials are ready and can be adapted into a grant proposal, pilot protocol, or collaborative project with the right team.

title: Immersive VR Rehabilitation for Multiple Sclerosis
text:
My prior VR experience
This project is not my first step into VR. Earlier in my career, I collaborated with Dr Ahmed Bentaleb and I co-authored:

Low-cost VR Collaborative System equipped with Haptic Feedback (ACM VRST)

In that work, we built a system where:

Multiple users join a shared VR environment as avatars

A Kinect sensor tracks body and gesture information

A haptic feedback system (microcontroller + vibrotactile motors + Wi-Fi) triggers physical sensations when avatars interact in VR

When one avatar “touches” another, the system maps that interaction to the real body and vibrates the corresponding motor, so the user actually feels the contact.
That experience gave me hands-on practice with:

VR engine integration (Unity)

Real-time networking and multi-user interaction

Designing and implementing haptic feedback hardware

Bridging virtual events and physical sensations

The MS rehab project builds directly on that foundation, but shifts the focus towards clinical and rehabilitation use cases.

Looking for collaborators
Right now, this project is concept + research plan + preliminary artifacts, not a completed clinical trial. That’s intentional: I decided not to rush a half-baked study without proper support.
I’m particularly interested in connecting with:

Clinicians and physical therapists working with MS patients

Labs focusing on neurorehabilitation, VR rehab, or tele-rehabilitation

Researchers looking for VR/AI/biomedical crossover projects

If you:

Have access to an MS patient population or rehab infrastructure, or

Are interested in co-developing a pilot study or grant around VR rehab

then I’d genuinely be happy to talk and see if we can move this project forward together.
You can find my contact info at the bottom of this page.

title: Immersive VR Rehabilitation for Multiple Sclerosis
section: Why this project matters to me
text:
Why this project matters to me
Beyond the academic and business side, this topic is personal. I have someone very close to me who lives with MS, and I’ve seen how the disease affects daily activities, motivation, and long-term planning.
That’s a big part of why I care about:

Rehabilitation that goes beyond “one-size-fits-all” exercises

Tools that can track progress, adapt to the person, and keep them engaged

Making use of VR not just as a gadget, but as a way to safely simulate real-world tasks and support both physical and mental health

title: Towards wearable, non-invasive and real-time hydration tracking
text:
HydroTrack is the first prototype I made by integrating a low-cost optical sensor into an open-source programmable watch and turning it into a hydration monitor.

Hardware – SparkFun AS7265x Triad spectroscopy sensor embedded in a DSTIKE Watch V4 (ESP32).

Experiments – Calibration with lab-grade spectrometer (Hach DR3900), electrolyte-solution benchmarking, skin-hydration tests during fasting & exercise.

Deployment – TinyML model runs fully on-device; LEDs indicate hydration state (green = hydrated, red = dehydrated).
